questions.question: What is the condition for total internal reflection to occur?

options.text: Light must travel from a rarer medium to a denser medium at an angle of 90°.
Light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.
Light must strike the boundary at 90° to the normal separating any two mediums of different refractive indices.
The refractive indices of both media must be equal.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Total Internal Reflection (TIR)** occurs when **light travels from a denser medium** (e.g., water or glass) to a **rarer medium** (e.g., air) and strikes the boundary at an angle **greater than the critical angle**.
 
• The **critical angle** is the minimum angle of incidence at which light is refracted along the boundary instead of passing into the second medium.
 
• If the angle of incidence exceeds the **critical angle**, the light is **completely reflected back** into the denser medium.
 
• The phenomenon depends on the **refractive indices** of the two media, and the critical angle can be calculated using the formula: **sin θ꜀ = n₂/n₁**, where **n₁** and **n₂** are the refractive indices of the denser and rarer media, respectively.
 
• The condition mentioned in the correct option is essential for applications like **fiber optics** and optical instruments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Critical Angle:**

 
 
• The critical angle is unique for different pairs of media. For example, the critical angle for light traveling from **water (n = 1.33)** to **air (n = 1)** is approximately **48.6°**.
 
• Light striking at an angle less than the critical angle will be refracted into the rarer medium.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Total Internal Reflection:**
 
 
• **Optical fibers:** Total internal reflection is the principle behind the transmission of light signals in **fiber optics**, enabling high-speed communication.
 
• **Mirage formation:** TIR explains how mirages occur in deserts due to varying air densities.
 
• **Prisms:** Prisms use TIR for light reflection in instruments like binoculars and periscopes.
 
 
 
• **Statement Analysis:**
 
 
• Statement 1: "Light must travel from a rarer medium to a denser medium at an angle of 90º." – *Incorrect*. TIR does not occur in this case; light is refracted instead.
 
• Statement 2: "Light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle." – *Correct*. This is the condition for TIR.
 
• Statement 3: "Light must strike the boundary at 90º to the normal separating any two mediums of different refractive indices." – *Incorrect*. At 90°, light travels perpendicularly and is transmitted without reflection.
 
• Statement 4: "The refractive indices of both media must be equal." – *Incorrect*. TIR requires different refractive indices for the two media.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fiber Optics:** TIR is the backbone of modern **telecommunication systems** using optical fibers, as it ensures minimal signal loss.
 
• **Examples:** Diamonds exhibit brilliance due to TIR of light within the gem.
 
• **Relevance:** TIR is crucial for understanding phenomena in physics, engineering, and medical technologies.
 
• **Innovation:** Devices like **endoscopes** use TIR for internal imaging in medical diagnostics.

• Project Starline integrates technologies like **3D depth cameras** and high-resolution displays to create a realistic holographic communication experience.
 
• The setup includes a specialized booth equipped with multiple cameras and sensors to capture and render a user’s **3D image in real time**.
 
• **Spatial audio** and lighting effects are synchronized with the video to make the interaction feel authentic and immersive.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Google Beam:**
 
 
• The platform has significant potential in the healthcare industry, enabling **doctors** to conduct remote consultations with a lifelike presence.
 
• In education, it can provide **immersive learning experiences** by facilitating realistic one-on-one or group interactions between teachers and students.
 
• Businesses can use this technology for better **virtual meetings** and collaborations, especially in global organizations where travel is impractical.

• Unlike video conferencing platforms such as Zoom or Teams, Project Starline creates a **3D holographic experience** that significantly reduces the feeling of distance.
 
• It eliminates typical issues like camera angles and screen boundaries, offering a more natural interaction.

• The system requires **specialized hardware** and a dedicated setup, which may limit its initial availability and accessibility to large organizations or specialized sectors.
 
• High data processing and bandwidth requirements may be another constraint in deploying this technology widely.

• **Revolution in Communication:** Project Starline marks a significant step forward in how we perceive virtual communication, bridging the gap between physical and virtual presence.

questions.question: What was the main objective of India’s First Five Year Plan (1951–56)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agricultural development**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The First Five-Year Plan of India (1951–56) focused primarily on **Agricultural development**. It emphasized increasing food production to address the issue of food scarcity and laid the foundation for agricultural modernization.
 
• The Plan was launched under the leadership of **Jawaharlal Nehru**, the first Prime Minister of India, and was based on the **Harrod-Domar model**, which prioritized investment in the agricultural sector.
 
• Agriculture contributed significantly to the Indian economy at that time, accounting for a majority of the GDP and employing the largest portion of the population. Hence, its development was a critical need.
 
• Key initiatives under the First Five-Year Plan included the establishment of major irrigation projects like the **Bhakra-Nangal Dam**, **DVC (Damodar Valley Corporation)**, and **Hirakud Dam** to improve water supply for agriculture.
 
• The Plan achieved success with a growth rate of **3.6%**, surpassing the target of 2.1%, largely due to favorable monsoons and the focus on agricultural productivity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Heavy Industrialization:**

 
 
• Although industrialization was a part of subsequent Five-Year Plans, the First Plan did not focus heavily on it. Industrial development gained prominence during the **Second Five-Year Plan**, which emphasized the growth of the public sector and heavy industries under the leadership of **Dr. P.C. Mahalanobis**.
 
• Examples of industries promoted later include steel plants in **Bhilai, Durgapur, and Rourkela**.
 
 
 
• **Privatization of PSUs:**
 
 
• Privatization of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) was not a focus during the First Five-Year Plan. In fact, the Plan emphasized the role of the **public sector** in national development.
 
• Privatization gained momentum in India much later, during the **1990s**, as part of economic reforms under the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** policy.
 
 
 
• **Growth of IT Services:**
 
 
• The development of Information Technology (IT) services was not a focus in the First Five-Year Plan. IT services began developing much later in India, particularly in the **1980s and 1990s**, with cities like **Bengaluru** emerging as IT hubs.
 
• Major initiatives in IT were introduced as part of **economic liberalization**, which encouraged private sector involvement and investment in technology.
 
 
 
• **First Five-Year Plan Highlights:**
 
 
• Objective: To address challenges like food shortages, poverty, and inflation.
 
• Sector Allocation: **44.6%** of the total budget was allocated to agriculture and irrigation.
 
• Achievements: Successful implementation of irrigation projects and agricultural modernization.
 
• Outcome: Laid the foundation for future economic and social development in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Five-Year Plans in India:**

 
 
• India adopted the concept of Five-Year Plans from the **Soviet Union**, aiming for systematic economic development.
 
• These plans were developed and monitored by the **Planning Commission**, which was established in **1950** by **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• The First Plan prioritized agriculture as India was primarily an agrarian economy with food shortages.
 
• Subsequent plans shifted focus to industrialization, infrastructure, and social development.
 
 
 
• **Bhakra-Nangal Dam:**
 
 
• One of the largest dam projects undertaken during the First Five-Year Plan.
 
• Located on the **Sutlej River**, it provides irrigation, hydropower, and flood control in northern India.
 
 
 
• **Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC):**
 
 
• Established in **1948**, DVC aimed to control floods, provide irrigation, and generate hydropower in the Damodar River basin.
 
• It served as a model for integrated resource management during the First Plan.

questions.question: Who was honoured with the Padma Bhushan in 2025 for their contributions to Indian cinema?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shekhar Kapur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Shekhar Kapur** was honored with the **Padma Bhushan** in the year **2025** for his outstanding contributions to **Indian cinema**.
 
• The **Padma Bhushan** is the third-highest civilian award in India, which recognizes distinguished service of a high order to the nation in any field.
 
• Shekhar Kapur is an internationally acclaimed filmmaker, known for his work in critically acclaimed movies such as **"Bandit Queen," "Elizabeth,"** and **"Elizabeth: The Golden Age."**
 
• He is celebrated for his cinematic storytelling, which often explores complex characters and deep historical narratives, earning him several accolades globally.
 
• The award was conferred upon him for his immense contribution to the Indian film industry, as well as his efforts to bring Indian cinema to the global stage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Shekhar Kapur:**

 
 
• Born on **6 December 1945**, Shekhar Kapur is an Indian filmmaker and actor known for his work in both Bollywood and Hollywood.
 
• His film **"Bandit Queen" (1994)** won the **National Film Award for Best Feature Film** in Hindi and gained international acclaim for its depiction of the life of Phoolan Devi.
 
• He directed the Oscar-winning historical drama **"Elizabeth" (1998)** and its sequel **"Elizabeth: The Golden Age" (2007).**
 
• Shekhar Kapur has also been a **UNICEF ambassador** and has contributed to several global humanitarian causes.
 
 
 
• **Padma Bhushan Award:**
 
 
• The Padma Bhushan is one of the **highest civilian awards** in India, instituted in **1954**.
 
• It is awarded to individuals for their exceptional service in various fields like **arts, literature, science, public affairs, sports, and social work**, among others.
 
• The awardees are announced annually on **Republic Day**, and the awards are presented by the **President of India**.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Contributions of Shekhar Kapur:**
 
 
• He served as the jury president of the **Cannes Film Festival** in 2010, showcasing his influence in global cinema.
 
• In addition to filmmaking, Kapur has been involved in several environmental and social initiatives, advocating for **sustainable development and water conservation**.
 
• He is also known for his work in documentaries, including a project on the **Dalai Lama**.
 
 
 
• **Padma Awards:**
 
 
• The Padma Awards are conferred in three categories: **Padma Vibhushan** (for exceptional and distinguished service), **Padma Bhushan** (distinguished service of higher order), and **Padma Shri** (distinguished service).
 
• These awards are aimed at recognizing individuals who have contributed significantly to their respective fields and have brought pride to the nation.
 
• Some other notable recipients of the Padma Bhushan include **Ratan Tata, Sachin Tendulkar, and Asha Bhosle**.

questions.question: Why is wheat grown in the north-western plains of India?

options.text: Because it lies close to the coastal water bodies
Because it receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon
Because the region has fertile alluvial soil and cool winters
Because the region has red soil with limited annual rainfall

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because the region has fertile alluvial soil and cool winters**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The north-western plains of India are known for their **fertile alluvial soil**, which is deposited by rivers like the **Ganga, Yamuna, Sutlej, and their tributaries**. This soil is rich in nutrients, making it highly suitable for wheat cultivation.
 
• Wheat requires a **cool climate during its growing season**, which the north-western plains provide during winter. The **temperatures range between 10°C to 15°C**, ideal for wheat germination and growth.
 
• The region experiences **adequate irrigation facilities** due to an extensive network of canals, ensuring water availability for wheat crops even during the dry season.
 
• Wheat is a rabi crop, meaning it is sown in winter and harvested in spring. The **low rainfall** during the wheat-growing season in the north-western plains prevents waterlogging, which is detrimental to the crop.
 
• The geographical location provides an advantage, as the plains have a **flat topography**, facilitating large-scale mechanized farming, which is beneficial for wheat cultivation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Alluvial Soil:**

 
 
• Alluvial soil is formed by the deposition of silt, sand, and clay by rivers. It is highly fertile and ideal for growing crops like wheat, rice, sugarcane, and pulses.
 
• The north-western plains have deep alluvial deposits, supporting extensive agricultural activities.
 
 
 
• **Wheat Crop:**
 
 
• Wheat is a **rabi crop**, sown in October-November and harvested in March-April.
 
• It requires a **temperature range of 10°C to 15°C** during germination and 20°C to 25°C during maturity.
 
• Wheat needs around **50-75 cm of annual rainfall**, making the climate of the north-western plains ideal for its growth.
 
• India is the second-largest producer of wheat globally, with major contributions from states like Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation in North-Western Plains:**
 
 
• The plains have a well-developed **canal irrigation system**, including the Indira Gandhi Canal and Bhakra Nangal Dam system.
 
• This ensures a consistent water supply for wheat cultivation, especially during the dry winter months.
 
 
 
• **Other Crops in the Region:**
 
 
• Besides wheat, the north-western plains are also suitable for growing crops like **rice, sugarcane, mustard, and cotton**.
 
• The availability of fertile soil and water resources makes this region an agricultural hub.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Red Soil and Limited Rainfall:**

 
 
• Red soil, commonly found in southern and eastern India, is not as fertile as alluvial soil and is not ideal for wheat cultivation.
 
• Limited rainfall in regions with red soil also makes it unsuitable for water-intensive crops like wheat.
 
 
 
• **Coastal Proximity:**
 
 
• Coastal regions are not conducive for wheat farming due to **high humidity and saline soil**.
 
• Wheat thrives in inland regions with less humidity and well-drained soil, such as the north-western plains.
 
 
 
• **Rainfall in Monsoon:**
 
 
• Wheat is a rabi crop and does not require heavy monsoon rains, which can damage the crop.
 
• Instead, it requires controlled irrigation during its growing season.

questions.question: Which of the following elements provides access to system settings, installed programs, and power options from the desktop?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Start Menu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Start Menu** is a core component of the Windows operating system and serves as a central hub for accessing system settings, installed programs, and power options directly from the desktop.
 
• Introduced in **Windows 95**, the Start Menu has evolved through various Windows versions to include features like search functionality, quick access to programs, and system utilities.
 
• The Start Menu provides easy navigation to essential system settings, such as **Control Panel, Settings**, and **Power Options**, enabling users to manage system configurations efficiently.
 
• It displays a list of installed applications, making it convenient for users to launch programs and access frequently used tools.
 
• The Start Menu also includes the **power options** (such as Shut Down, Restart, and Sleep), allowing users to manage the system state effortlessly.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Taskbar:**

 
 
• The **Taskbar** is located at the bottom of the screen in Windows operating systems.
 
• It provides quick access to open applications and pinned programs but does not directly offer access to system settings or power options.
 
• Features include the **Notification Area**, system tray, and quick launch icons.
 
 
 
• **File Explorer:**
 
 
• **File Explorer** is a file management application in Windows used to browse, access, and organize files and folders on the computer.
 
• It does not provide direct access to system settings or power options.
 
• Commonly used for tasks like copying, moving, and deleting files.
 
 
 
• **Notification Area:**
 
 
• The **Notification Area**, also known as the system tray, displays icons for background applications, system notifications, and shortcuts like volume control and network status.
 
• While it provides quick access to certain system features, it does not serve as a hub for accessing system settings, installed programs, or power options.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of the Start Menu:**
 
 
• Over the years, the Start Menu has been enhanced with features like **live tiles** in Windows 8 and **search integration** in Windows 10.
 
• Windows 11 introduced a more streamlined design and centralized layout for the Start Menu.
 
 
 
• **Power Options:**
 
 
• Power options are essential for managing the computer's energy consumption, allowing users to shut down, restart, or put the system into sleep mode.
 
• These options are conveniently located within the Start Menu, ensuring easy access.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Windows Versions:**

 
 
• Each Windows version since **Windows 95** has included a Start Menu, with design modifications enhancing user experience.
 
• Windows 8 temporarily replaced the Start Menu with the Start Screen, but it returned in Windows 10 due to user demand.
 
 
 
• **Accessibility:**
 
 
• The Start Menu is accessible via the **Windows key** or by clicking the Start icon located on the Taskbar.
 
• It can be customized with pinned applications, shortcuts, and folders for quick access.
 
 
 
• **Search Integration:**
 
 
• The Start Menu incorporates a **search bar**, allowing users to quickly locate files, programs, or system settings.
 
• This feature streamlines navigation and enhances productivity.

questions.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) about the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution of India?

options.text: The President of India has the ultimate authority to approve or reject constitutional amendments independently.
The Parliament cannot amend any part of the Constitution under any circumstances.
The Parliament can amend the Constitution, but it cannot change or destroy its basic structure or essential features.
The Parliament has unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights.

questions.solution: The correct answer is __**The Parliament can amend the Constitution, but it cannot change or destroy its basic structure or essential features.**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • The **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala** case (1973) is one of the most significant judgments in Indian constitutional history. • The Supreme Court laid down the **"Basic Structure Doctrine"**, which restricts the power of the Parliament to amend the Constitution in a way that alters its fundamental structure. • According to the judgment, while the Parliament has the authority under **Article 368** of the Indian Constitution to amend any part of the Constitution, it cannot alter or destroy its basic structure or essential features. • The basic structure includes principles such as the supremacy of the Constitution, separation of powers, fundamental rights, and the rule of law. • This doctrine ensures that the core principles of the Indian Constitution remain preserved, even as the Constitution evolves through amendments.

questions.question: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court uphold the Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right in 2017?

options.text: Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India
Indira Sawhney vs. Union of India
Navtej Singh Johar vs. Union of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Puttaswamy vs. Union of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Puttaswamy vs. Union of India case**, decided in **2017**, was a landmark judgment by the Supreme Court of India. It affirmed the **Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right** under the Constitution of India.
 
• The case was led by **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy**, a retired judge, who challenged the **Aadhaar scheme** on the grounds of privacy infringement.
 
• The judgment ruled that the **Right to Privacy** is protected as an intrinsic part of the **Right to Life and Personal Liberty** under **Article 21** and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by **Part III of the Constitution**.
 
• A nine-judge bench unanimously agreed that privacy is a fundamental right, overturning previous judgments that denied this status.
 
• This case laid the foundation for future decisions related to privacy, data protection, and individual rights in India. It set a precedent for protecting citizens' privacy against state and private encroachments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India:**

 
 
• This case, decided in **2015**, struck down **Section 66A** of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which was deemed unconstitutional for violating the **freedom of speech and expression** under **Article 19(1)(a)**.
 
• It did not address the **Right to Privacy**. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Indira Sawhney vs. Union of India:**
 
 
• This landmark case from **1992** dealt with the issue of **reservation quotas** for socially and educationally backward classes and upheld the **Mandal Commission recommendations**.
 
• It was not related to the **Right to Privacy**. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Navtej Singh Johar vs. Union of India:**
 
 
• Decided in **2018**, this case struck down **Section 377** of the Indian Penal Code, decriminalizing consensual homosexual acts.
 
• While it emphasized dignity and privacy, the judgment did not specifically focus on the **Right to Privacy** as a fundamental right. Hence, this option is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Right to Privacy:**
 
 
• The concept of privacy is rooted in the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)**, which India is a signatory to.
 
• It gained prominence in Indian jurisprudence after the **Puttaswamy case**, ensuring safeguards against misuse of personal data and state surveillance.
 
• The judgment has implications for laws related to **data protection, surveillance, and Aadhaar**, shaping India's digital privacy framework.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 21:**

 
 
• Enshrines the **Right to Life and Personal Liberty**, which includes the **Right to Privacy**.
 
• It serves as the basis for protecting individual autonomy and dignity in India.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Puttaswamy Judgment:**
 
 
• Influenced legislation related to **data protection and privacy**, such as the **Personal Data Protection Bill**.
 
• The judgment has been cited in subsequent cases, including those concerning **Aadhaar** and **internet shutdowns**.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Bench:**
 
 
• The case was decided by a **nine-judge bench**, illustrating its constitutional significance.
 
• It overturned previous judgments like **Kharak Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh**, which denied privacy as a fundamental right.

questions.question: Which mode of transport is most suitable for transporting heavy and bulky goods over long distances?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Railways**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Railways** is the most suitable mode of transport for heavy and bulky goods over long distances because it is cost-effective and efficient for transporting large volumes of goods.
 
• It provides a reliable and safe means of transport for commodities such as coal, steel, cement, and agricultural produce.
 
• Railways are equipped with specialized freight wagons that can carry heavy loads and ensure the goods' safety during transit.
 
• It is an environmentally friendly mode of transport with lower carbon emissions compared to roadways or airways.
 
• Railway networks are well-developed in countries like **India, the United States, and China**, which makes them a vital part of the economy and trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pipelines:**

 
 
• Used to transport liquids like oil, natural gas, and water.
 
• Efficient for specific industries but not suitable for general heavy and bulky goods.
 
 
 
• **Roadways:**
 
 
• Flexible and accessible for short to medium distances.
 
• Not cost-effective for heavy goods or long-distance transportation due to higher fuel and maintenance costs.
 
 
 
• **Airways:**
 
 
• Best for fast and time-sensitive deliveries but very expensive.
 
• Not suitable for bulky and heavy goods due to weight limitations and high freight charges.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Railways:**
 
 
• Railways can carry goods in bulk over long distances at a lower cost per unit compared to road or air transport.
 
• They are vital for the economic development of a country as they facilitate the movement of raw materials and finished goods.
 
• Examples include the **Indian Railways**, which is one of the largest railway networks in the world, and the **Trans-Siberian Railway** in Russia, which connects Europe and Asia.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Importance of Railways:**

 
 
• The railways contribute significantly to reducing transportation costs, thereby lowering the overall cost of goods.
 
• In **India**, the **Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC)** is an ambitious project aimed at improving the efficiency of goods transport via rail.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Benefits:**
 
 
• Railways are more energy-efficient and produce significantly less pollution compared to road and air transport.
 
• Countries are increasingly investing in **electrified rail networks** to further reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines impulse in mechanics?

options.text: The product of mass and velocity
The product of force and the time for which it acts
The rate of change of momentum multiplied by the distance
The change in displacement over time

questions.question:
Which of the following statements regarding the Ryotwari settlement is correct?

1.It was developed by Thomas Munro.

2. The settlement was made directly with the cultivators, not zamindars.

3.It was tested on a small scale in the annexed territories of Tipu.

4. Finding it successful, it was then applied in the Ganga plains.

Select the correct combination:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1, 2, and 3 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Ryotwari settlement was developed by Thomas Munro**, a British administrator. He introduced this system in the Madras Presidency in 1820. Under this system, the revenue settlement was made directly with the individual cultivators or ryots, bypassing the zamindars. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **The settlement was made directly with the cultivators** under the Ryotwari system. Unlike the Zamindari system, where zamindars acted as intermediaries, the Ryotwari system established a direct relationship between the British government and the farmers. This ensured that the farmers were responsible for paying land revenue directly to the state. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• The Ryotwari system was **tested on a small scale in the annexed territories of Tipu Sultan**. These territories, which came under British control after Tipu's defeat, served as experimental grounds for the new settlement system. It was considered a success and later expanded. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The assertion that the Ryotwari system was applied in the Ganga plains is incorrect. The Ryotwari system was primarily implemented in regions such as Madras, Bombay, and parts of Assam. The Ganga plains were primarily under the Zamindari settlement. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Therefore, the correct answer is 1, 2, and 3 only.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ryotwari System:**

 
 
• Introduced during British rule, this system focused on direct revenue collection from farmers or cultivators (ryots).
 
• The system was implemented in areas where there were no large landlords or zamindars, such as Madras, Bombay, and parts of Assam.
 
• The revenue rates were fixed based on the fertility and productivity of the land and were subject to periodic revisions.
 
• It ensured that the cultivators had ownership rights over the land as long as they paid the required revenue.
 
 
 
• **Zamindari System:**
 
 
• Another land revenue system implemented by the British in regions such as Bengal, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• In this system, zamindars acted as intermediaries between the British government and the cultivators, collecting revenue from farmers and paying it to the state.
 
• This system often led to exploitation of farmers by zamindars, as they charged high rents.
 
 
 
• **Mahalwari System:**
 
 
• Introduced in North India, especially in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and parts of Madhya Pradesh.
 
• Under this system, land revenue was collected from groups of villages (mahal) rather than individual cultivators.
 
• The headman of the mahal was responsible for collecting revenue on behalf of the group.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Land Revenue Systems:**
 
 
• The Ryotwari system emphasized direct settlement, which reduced intermediaries but placed the burden of revenue payment directly on the cultivators.
 
• The Zamindari system involved intermediaries, leading to exploitation but ensured a structured revenue collection process.
 
• The Mahalwari system combined aspects of both, focusing on group settlements and revenue collection.
 
 
 
• **Historical Impact:**
 
 
• The Ryotwari system provided ownership rights to cultivators but failed during famines as farmers struggled to pay fixed revenue.
 
• The Zamindari system led to the rise of powerful landlord classes but also increased the exploitation of farmers.
 
• All systems significantly influenced land revenue policies in colonial India, shaping socio-economic conditions of the time.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Thomas Munro:**

 
 
• He was the Governor of Madras Presidency from 1820 to 1827.
 
• Played a key role in the development and implementation of the Ryotwari system.
 
 
 
• **Revenue Collection:**
 
 
• Under Ryotwari, revenue collection was based on the land's productivity, making it variable.
 
• The fixed revenue rates became a burden during periods of drought or famine.
 
 
 
• **Regions of Implementation:**
 
 
• Ryotwari was prominent in Madras, Bombay, and Assam.
 
• Zamindari dominated Bengal, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• Mahalwari was implemented in Punjab and northern regions.
 
 
 
• **Colonial Policies:**
 
 
• These systems were designed primarily to maximize revenue for the British government.
 
• They had long-term implications for agricultural practices and rural economies in India.

questions.question: What was the other name of Chandragupta II, the renowned ruler of the Gupta dynasty?

• **Chandragupta II**, a prominent ruler of the **Gupta dynasty**, was also known by the title **Vikramaditya**. This title symbolized his valor and administrative excellence.
 
• He ruled during the period of **375–415 CE**, a time considered the **Golden Age of India** due to advancements in science, art, and culture.

__
 
• **Gupta Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Gupta Empire was founded by **Chandragupta I** around **320 CE**. It is regarded as one of the most influential empires in Indian history.
 
• The period of the Gupta dynasty is often referred to as the **Golden Age of India** due to the remarkable achievements in art, literature, architecture, and science.

• **Contributions of Chandragupta II:**

• **Defeat of Saka Rulers:**
 
 
• Chandragupta II is credited with defeating the **Saka rulers**, also known as the Western Kshatrapas, and annexing their territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Golden Age of India:** The Gupta period is termed the **Golden Age** due to unprecedented achievements in **science, mathematics, astronomy, literature, and architecture**.
 
• **Kalidasa's Works:** Renowned works such as **Shakuntala** and **Meghaduta** were composed during Chandragupta II’s reign.

questions.question: Amir Khusrau is known for contributing to which two languages?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Amir Khusrau** was a renowned **Sufi musician, poet, and scholar** in medieval India, often referred to as the "Parrot of India".
 
• He is known for his significant contributions to **Persian** and **Hindavi** (an early form of Hindi and Urdu), which laid the foundation for the development of Urdu language.
 
• He wrote extensively in **Persian**, composing various poems, riddles, and prose, which enriched Indo-Persian literature.
 
• Khusrau is credited with introducing Hindavi into his works, blending Persian and local Indian languages, creating a fusion of linguistic traditions.
 
• His works in **Hindavi** include riddles, songs, and couplets, making him a pioneer in developing the vernacular tradition in Indian literature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Persian Language:**

 
 
• **Persian** was widely used as the court language during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal period.
 
• Amir Khusrau's Persian poetry includes **Ghazals, Masnavis, and Rubaiyat**, showcasing themes of love, spirituality, and philosophy.
 
• His Persian works include **Tughluq Nama**, **Qiran-us-Sa’dain**, and **Khazain-ul-Futuh**.
 
• Persian became a medium for administrative purposes and literary creativity during Khusrau's era.
 
 
 
• **Hindavi Language:**
 
 
• **Hindavi** was an early form of Hindi and Urdu, and Amir Khusrau is regarded as one of its early proponents.
 
• Khusrau's Hindavi works include riddles, folk songs, and couplets that reflect the socio-cultural milieu of his time.
 
• His Hindavi compositions were enjoyed by both the elite and the common people, popularizing local dialects in literature.
 
• Hindavi later evolved into modern Hindi and Urdu, forming the basis of contemporary North Indian languages.
 
 
 
• **Amir Khusrau’s Legacy:**
 
 
• He is credited with creating the **qawwali** genre, blending Persian and Indian musical traditions.
 
• Khusrau introduced new instruments like the **tabla** and popularized the sitar during his time.
 
• His contributions to literature and music earned him the title of **“Father of Urdu Literature”**.
 
• He was a disciple of Sufi saint **Nizamuddin Auliya**, and his works reflect a deep spiritual essence.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Options:**

 
 
• **Sanskrit and Tamil:** These languages have ancient roots and are unrelated to Khusrau’s works. They were primarily used for religious and classical literature in India.
 
• **Bengali and Punjabi:** These regional languages have distinct literary traditions and were not influenced by Khusrau’s contributions.
 
• **Marathi and Gujarati:** These languages belong to different linguistic families and regions than those influenced by Khusrau.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Khusrau’s Work:**
 
 
• His innovative blending of Persian and Hindavi laid the foundation for the **syncretic culture** of India.
 
• Through literature and music, Khusrau played a crucial role in fostering cultural harmony during his era.

questions.question: The Human Development Index emphasises people-centric development. Who is credited with creating the HDI alongside Amartya Sen?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahbub ul Haq**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mahbub ul Haq**, a Pakistani economist, is credited alongside **Amartya Sen** for creating the **Human Development Index (HDI)**.
 
• The **Human Development Index (HDI)** was introduced in the first **Human Development Report (HDR)** published in **1990** by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)**.
 
• The HDI focuses on measuring a country's development by combining three key dimensions: **life expectancy, education level, and standard of living**.
 
• Mahbub ul Haq conceptualized this index to shift the focus of development economics from national income accounting to **people-centered policies**.
 
• **Amartya Sen**, an Indian economist, contributed by providing the theoretical framework emphasizing **capabilities and freedoms** as essential aspects of human development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Human Development Index (HDI):**

 
 
• The HDI is a composite index that measures average achievement in three basic dimensions of human development:
 
• **Health:** Measured by life expectancy at birth.
 
• **Education:** Measured by mean years of schooling for adults aged 25 years or more and expected years of schooling for children entering school.
 
• **Standard of Living:** Measured by gross national income (GNI) per capita (adjusted for purchasing power parity).
 
 
 
• **Mahbub ul Haq:**
 
 
• He was a renowned **Pakistani economist** and policy-maker, born in **1934** and passed away in **1998**.
 
• Haq's work on the HDI was inspired by his vision to create a development model that prioritizes **human welfare** over mere economic growth.
 
• He also served as the **Director of the Human Development Report Office** at the UNDP.
 
 
 
• **Amartya Sen:**
 
 
• Sen is an **Indian economist and philosopher**, awarded the **Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences** in **1998**.
 
• His **capability approach** emphasizes the importance of enabling individuals to achieve well-being through freedom of choice.
 
• Sen's theoretical contributions were crucial for the development of the HDI framework.
 
 
 
• **Importance of HDI:**
 
 
• The HDI provides a broad measure of human development that goes beyond economic performance indicators like GDP.
 
• It helps policymakers understand the multidimensional aspects of development and design **people-centered policies**.
 
• Countries are ranked on a scale of 0 to 1, where higher values indicate better human development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Criticism of HDI:**

 
 
• The HDI has been criticized for being too simplistic, as it does not consider other critical dimensions like **environmental sustainability, political freedom, and inequality**.
 
• Despite its limitations, the HDI remains a widely used and influential tool for assessing and comparing human development across countries.
 
 
 
• **UNDP and Human Development Reports:**
 
 
• The **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** publishes annual Human Development Reports to provide insights into global and regional development trends.
 
• These reports use the HDI as a central measure to assess progress and highlight challenges in achieving sustainable human development.

questions.question: Which constitutional Articles ensure the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts for enforcing fundamental rights, including RTI?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Articles 32 and 226**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 32**: This article empowers the **Supreme Court** to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. It is often referred to as the "heart and soul of the Constitution" as described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• **Article 226**: This article empowers the **High Courts** to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights as well as for any other purpose, making it broader in scope compared to Article 32.
 
• Both these articles are crucial in ensuring the protection and enforcement of fundamental rights enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Under these provisions, courts can issue writs such as **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto**, ensuring judicial intervention in cases of rights violations.
 
• Additionally, the **Right to Information (RTI)** is considered a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution, which guarantees the right to freedom of speech and expression. Articles 32 and 226 provide the legal framework to enforce this right.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Writs under Articles 32 and 226:**

 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** Protects an individual's right to liberty by directing the release of a person unlawfully detained.
 
• **Mandamus:** Orders a public authority to perform a duty it is bound to do.
 
• **Prohibition:** Prevents lower courts or tribunals from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari:** Quashes the order of a lower court or tribunal which exceeds its jurisdiction or violates procedural fairness.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** Challenges the legality of a person's claim to a public office.
 
 
 
• **Scope of Article 32:**
 
 
• Article 32 applies exclusively to the **Supreme Court**.
 
• It deals with cases concerning the violation of **fundamental rights**.
 
• It is a guaranteed remedy, meaning that the Supreme Court is bound to act if fundamental rights are violated.
 
 
 
• **Scope of Article 226:**
 
 
• Article 226 applies to **High Courts** and has a broader scope than Article 32.
 
• High Courts can issue writs not only for the enforcement of fundamental rights but also for any other legal right.
 
• The jurisdiction of High Courts is wider but subject to territorial and other constraints.
 
 
 
• **Right to Information (RTI):**
 
 
• The **RTI Act, 2005**, allows Indian citizens to request information from public authorities, enhancing transparency and accountability.
 
• It is linked to **Article 19(1)(a)**, which guarantees the right to freedom of speech and expression.
 
• Under Articles 32 and 226, individuals can approach courts if their right to information is denied.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Articles 32 and 226: Comparison**:

 
 
• Article 32 is a **fundamental right**, while Article 226 is a constitutional provision.
 
• Article 32 provides remedies for **fundamental rights violations**, while Article 226 extends to other legal rights as well.
 
• Under Article 226, High Courts have jurisdiction over matters within their respective states, whereas Article 32 gives the Supreme Court jurisdiction over the entire country.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Activism:**
 
 
• The powers under Articles 32 and 226 are instrumental for judicial activism in India.
 
• These articles empower courts to ensure the implementation of constitutional rights and address grievances of individuals.

questions.question: What is the value of one roentgen (R) when expressed in SI units?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2) 2.58×10-4 coulombs per kilogram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **roentgen (R)** is a unit of exposure for X-rays and gamma rays. It measures the amount of ionization produced in air by these types of radiation.
 
• In the **International System of Units (SI)**, exposure is quantified in terms of charge per unit mass, specifically in coulombs per kilogram (C/kg).
 
• The value of **1 roentgen** is defined as **2.58×10-4 coulombs per kilogram (C/kg)** in SI units. This is the amount of electric charge produced by gamma or X-rays in 1 kg of air under standard conditions.
 
• Option 1 (1.0×10-3 grays) is incorrect because **gray (Gy)** is a unit of absorbed dose, not exposure. It measures energy absorbed per kilogram of matter, unlike roentgen, which measures ionization in air.
 
• Option 3 (1.6×10-19 coulombs) is incorrect because this value refers to the charge of an electron, unrelated to the roentgen unit.
 
• Option 4 (3.7×1010 disintegrations per second) is incorrect because it represents the activity of a radioactive source, measured in becquerels (Bq), not exposure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Roentgen (R):**

 
 
• Named after **Wilhelm Röntgen**, who discovered X-rays in 1895.
 
• It is a historical unit used to measure exposure to ionizing radiation in air.
 
• One roentgen corresponds to the amount of radiation that produces 2.58×10-4 C/kg of air.
 
 
 
• **SI Units for Radiation:**
 
 
• The **coulomb per kilogram (C/kg)** is the SI unit for exposure, replacing the roentgen in modern systems.
 
• Other related units include the **gray (Gy)** for absorbed dose and the **sievert (Sv)** for dose equivalent, which considers biological effects.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Units:**
 
 
• **Gray (Gy):** Measures energy deposited by radiation in a material, 1 Gy = 1 joule/kg.
 
• **Roentgen (R):** Measures ionization in air, 1 R = 2.58×10-4 C/kg.
 
• **Becquerel (Bq):** Measures activity, indicating the number of disintegrations per second.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• The roentgen is used in medical imaging and radiation safety to quantify exposure.
 
• It helps in calibrating radiation detection devices and ensuring safe levels of radiation in environments like hospitals and nuclear facilities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ionizing Radiation:**

 
 
• Includes X-rays, gamma rays, and other high-energy particles capable of ionizing atoms in matter.
 
• Measured in units like roentgen (R), gray (Gy), and sievert (Sv), depending on the context (exposure, absorbed dose, or biological effect).
 
 
 
• **Radiation Safety Standards:**
 
 
• Limits on radiation exposure are established by organizations like the **International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP)**.
 
• Occupational exposure for radiation workers is typically limited to **20 mSv/year** averaged over five years.
 
 
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• 1 R = 2.58×10-4 C/kg.
 
• 1 Gy = 100 rad (older unit of absorbed dose).
 
• 1 Sv = 100 rem (older unit of dose equivalent).

questions.question: The introduction of English education in India was promoted through which of the following documents?

__
 
• **Macaulay's Minute**, written by **Thomas Babington Macaulay** in **1835**, emphasized the introduction of English education in India. He argued for the replacement of traditional Indian education systems with English-based education.
 
• The Minute proposed creating a class of Indians who were "Indian in blood and color, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect," to act as intermediaries between the British rulers and Indian society.
 
• This document led to the establishment of English as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges, particularly in higher education institutions.
 
• The Minute was critical in shaping the colonial education policy, moving away from indigenous systems of knowledge and prioritizing European literature and sciences.
 
• Lord William Bentinck, the Governor-General of India at the time, officially adopted Macaulay's recommendations, making English the primary language for education and administration in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Charter Act of 1813:**

 
 
• The Charter Act of 1813 was one of the earliest legislations to officially recognize the importance of education in India.
 
• It allocated **Rs. 1 lakh** annually for the promotion of education and authorized the Christian missionaries to spread English education.
 
• However, it did not lay down a clear framework for the implementation of English education, leaving it as a general policy.
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act:**
 
 
• The Regulating Act of 1773 primarily focused on administrative reforms and did not directly address education.
 
• Its purpose was to regulate the functioning of the East India Company and ensure accountability in governance.
 
 
 
• **Pitts India Act:**
 
 
• The Pitts India Act of 1784 was another administrative reform act, aiming to improve the control of the British Crown over the East India Company.
 
• It did not include any provisions related to education or the introduction of English in India.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Macaulay’s Minute:**
 
 
• The Minute led to the establishment of institutions like **Delhi College** and **Calcutta Medical College**, which adopted English as the medium of instruction.
 
• The focus shifted towards Western literature, science, and philosophy, sidelining traditional Indian systems of education.
 
• This policy contributed significantly to the formation of an educated middle class in India, which later played a vital role in the Indian independence movement.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Macaulay's Views:**

 
 
• Macaulay believed that English education would modernize India and create a class of individuals capable of bridging the gap between the British rulers and Indian society.
 
• His views sparked debates on the impact of colonial education, with critics arguing that it undermined Indian culture and traditional knowledge systems.
 
 
 
• **Long-Term Impact:**
 
 
• The introduction of English education significantly influenced the socio-political landscape of India, fostering a new wave of intellectual and political thought.
 
• It also contributed to the growth of nationalist movements by enabling Indians to study Western political philosophies and ideologies.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Minute was written during the early 19th century, a period marked by British attempts to consolidate their control over India through socio-cultural interventions.
 
• It reflected the colonial belief in the superiority of Western culture and its ability to 'civilize' colonized societies.

questions.question: What is the primary cause of southwest monsoon in India?

options.text: Differential heating of land and sea

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Differential heating of land and sea**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The southwest monsoon in India is primarily caused by the **differential heating of land and sea**. During summer, the Indian subcontinent, especially the northern plains, heats up faster than the surrounding oceans, creating a low-pressure area over the land.
 
• The **Indian Ocean**, on the other hand, remains relatively cooler. This temperature difference causes moisture-laden winds to blow from the high-pressure area over the ocean to the low-pressure area over the land.
 
• The monsoon winds are further intensified by the **Coriolis effect**, which deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. This shifts the winds from the southwest direction, giving them their name.
 
• The monsoon winds pick up moisture from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, leading to heavy rainfall in various parts of India, especially along the western coast and northeastern states.
 
• The southwest monsoon is a critical climatic phenomenon for India as it provides about **75-90% of the annual rainfall** in most regions, supporting agriculture and water resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Option 1: Tidal effects**

 
 
• Tidal effects are caused by the gravitational forces exerted by the **Moon and the Sun** on Earth's water bodies. While tides influence coastal ecosystems, they have no significant role in the formation of the southwest monsoon.
 
• Tides result in periodic changes in sea levels but do not contribute to large-scale wind patterns or precipitation.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Westerly winds from the Atlantic**
 
 
• The westerly winds from the Atlantic Ocean primarily affect the weather patterns of Europe and North America. These winds are unrelated to the Indian monsoon system.
 
• The southwest monsoon in India is driven by seasonal wind patterns over the Indian Ocean and not by the westerly winds originating from the Atlantic.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Local winds from the desert**
 
 
• While local winds like the **loo** (hot, dry winds) are significant during the summer in northern India, they are not responsible for the monsoon.
 
• Such winds have a localized impact and contribute to high temperatures but do not influence the large-scale monsoon system.
 
 
 
• **Monsoon Onset and Withdrawal**
 
 
• The southwest monsoon usually begins in **June** and lasts until **September**. It first hits the Kerala coast and then advances northward.
 
• The withdrawal of the monsoon begins in September, starting from the northwestern parts of India.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Monsoon**
 
 
• The monsoon is vital for India's **agriculture**, which employs a significant portion of the population. Crops like rice, sugarcane, and cotton are dependent on monsoon rains.
 
• It also replenishes reservoirs, lakes, and groundwater, which are crucial for drinking water and hydroelectric power generation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The southwest monsoon accounts for around **70-90% of India's total annual rainfall**, making it a crucial climatic event for the country.
 
• The **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**, a low-pressure zone near the equator, shifts northward during summer, further aiding the monsoon winds.
 
• The **Western Ghats** and the **Himalayas** significantly influence monsoon rainfall distribution. The Western Ghats cause orographic rainfall, while the Himalayas block the monsoon winds, ensuring rain over the northern plains.
 
• Climate phenomena like **El Niño** and **La Niña** can impact the intensity of the monsoon. El Niño typically weakens the monsoon, leading to drought-like conditions in India.
 
• Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) monitors and predicts monsoon patterns, which are critical for agricultural planning and disaster management.

• A **scramjet engine** (Supersonic Combustion Ramjet) is an advanced air-breathing propulsion system designed to operate at **supersonic speeds**.

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for causing convectional rainfall?

options.text: Intense surface heating causing air to rise
Cold and warm air masses meeting

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Intense surface heating causing air to rise**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Convectional rainfall occurs due to **intense surface heating**, which causes the air to rise vertically. This rising air cools and condenses to form clouds, resulting in rainfall.
 
• This type of rainfall is common in **equatorial regions**, where temperatures are high throughout the year, leading to frequent intense heating of the surface.
 
• It generally occurs in areas with **low-pressure systems**, where the heated air rises freely without obstruction.
 
• Convectional rainfall usually happens during the **afternoon or early evening** when the surface heating is at its peak.
 
• This process results in **short-lived but intense rainfall**, often accompanied by thunder and lightning due to the rapid condensation of moisture in the atmosphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cyclonic Movements:**

 
 
• Cyclonic rainfall occurs due to the interaction of air masses in a cyclone, which results in lifting and cooling of warm, moist air.
 
• This type of rainfall is widespread and sustained, unlike convectional rainfall. *(Incorrect for convectional rainfall)*
 
 
 
• **Mountains forcing air to rise:**
 
 
• Orographic or relief rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over mountains or elevated terrains.
 
• As the air rises, it cools and condenses, causing rainfall on the windward side of the mountain. *(Incorrect for convectional rainfall)*
 
 
 
• **Cold and warm air masses meeting:**
 
 
• This mechanism leads to frontal rainfall, which occurs at the meeting point of cold and warm air masses.
 
• Frontal rainfall is generally associated with temperate regions, and the rain is more widespread. *(Incorrect for convectional rainfall)*
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of convectional rainfall:**
 
 
• It is highly localized and occurs over small areas.
 
• It is most prominent during the summer months when surface heating is at its maximum.
 
• Regions like the **Amazon Basin** and parts of Africa experience convectional rainfall regularly.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Global Examples:**

 
 
• Equatorial regions such as the **Amazon Rainforest**, Congo Basin, and Indonesia experience convectional rainfall due to high temperatures and intense heating.
 
• Temperate regions may experience convectional rainfall during the summer months.
 
 
 
• **Associated Weather Conditions:**
 
 
• Convectional rainfall is often accompanied by **thunderstorms**, strong winds, and lightning due to the rapid upward movement of air.
 
• Cloud formations such as **cumulonimbus clouds** are common during convectional rainfall.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• This type of rainfall is crucial for sustaining tropical rainforests and supporting biodiversity in equatorial regions.
 
• It also plays a role in replenishing groundwater in localized areas.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution states that Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 37**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 37** of the Indian Constitution explicitly states that the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are fundamental in governance but are **not enforceable by any court of law**.
 
• The DPSP are outlined in **Part IV** of the Indian Constitution and are intended to guide the government in formulating policies and laws to establish a just society.
 
• While these principles are non-justiciable, they act as a moral and ethical framework for lawmakers to ensure the welfare of citizens.
 
• Article 37 emphasizes that the implementation of these principles is crucial for achieving the goals set in the Preamble of the Constitution, such as **justice, equality, and liberty**.
 
• The non-enforceability of DPSP differentiates them from Fundamental Rights, which are outlined in **Part III** of the Constitution and are enforceable by courts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSP are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and reflect the ideals of socio-economic democracy.
 
• They aim to create a welfare state by addressing issues like **health, education, poverty alleviation, women empowerment, and equitable distribution of resources**.
 
• Examples of DPSP include provisions related to **free legal aid, environmental protection, promotion of education, and fair distribution of wealth**.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights vs. DPSP:**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enforceable by courts and protect individual liberties, while DPSP provide guidelines for governance.
 
• In case of conflict, the judiciary often balances both, ensuring that neither is undermined significantly.
 
 
 
• **Judiciary and DPSP:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court of India has emphasized the importance of DPSP in cases like **Minerva Mills vs. Union of India (1980)** to ensure harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP.
 
• DPSP are considered dynamic and are often updated through amendments to reflect contemporary socio-economic issues.
 
 
 
• **Examples of DPSP Implementation:**
 
 
• Initiatives like **National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA)** and **Right to Education Act** align with the goals of DPSP.
 
• Environmental laws and policies in India are often inspired by the directive principles advocating sustainable development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** The DPSP were included in the Constitution to ensure socio-economic justice and were influenced by the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and the **Directive Principles of Irish Constitution**.
 
• **Constitutional Amendments:** Various amendments, such as the **42nd Amendment Act (1976)**, have expanded the scope of DPSP.
 
• **Examples:** Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, and 43 are key DPSP provisions addressing issues like equal pay, protection of children, and judicial access.

For a number to be divisible by 22, it must be divisible by both 2 and 11.

Divisibility by 2: The number must be even (eliminates 6136901).

Divisibility by 11: The difference of the sum of alternate digits must be 0 or a multiple of 11.

Testing 7467614: (4 + 6 + 6 + 7) − (1 + 7 + 4) = 23 − 12 = 11.

**∴ The correct answer is 7467614.**

**Given:**

Options: 7467614, 6136901, 6580350, 8132950

**Formula Used:**

Divisibility by 22: A number is divisible by 22 if it is exactly divisible by 2 and 11.

Divisibility by 2: The unit digit must be an even number (0, 2, 4, 6, or 8).

Divisibility by 11: The difference between the sum of digits at odd places and the sum of digits at even places must be 0 or a multiple of 11.

**Calculations:**

⇒ Check divisibility by 2: 7467614, 6580350, and 8132950 end with an even digit, so they are divisible by 2.

⇒ The number 6136901 ends in 1, so it is odd and can be eliminated.

⇒ Check divisibility by 11 for the remaining numbers:

⇒ Option 1 (7467614): Sum of odd places = 4 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 23. Sum of even places = 1 + 7 + 4 = 12. Difference = 23 − 12 = 11. (Divisible by 11)

⇒ Option 3 (6580350): Sum of odd places = 0 + 3 + 8 + 6 = 17. Sum of even places = 5 + 0 + 5 = 10. Difference = 17 − 10 = 7. (Not divisible by 11)

⇒ Option 4 (8132950): Sum of odd places = 0 + 9 + 3 + 8 = 20. Sum of even places = 5 + 2 + 1 = 8. Difference = 20 − 8 = 12. (Not divisible by 11)

⇒ Therefore, only the number 7467614 satisfies both conditions.

**∴ The correct answer is 7467614.**

Divisibility Rule for Composite Numbers

To check divisibility by any composite number, break it down into co-prime factors and check the divisibility for each factor individually (e.g., for 72, check 8 and 9).

Divisibility Rule for 3 and 9

A number is divisible by 3 or 9 if the sum of all its individual digits is a multiple of 3 or 9, respectively.

Divisibility Rule for 4 and 8

A number is divisible by 4 if the last two digits form a number divisible by 4. It is divisible by 8 if the last three digits form a number divisible by 8.

questions.question: If the 6-digit number N01M22 is divisible by 11, then which of the options below can give a possible correct relation between M and N?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

For divisibility by 11, the difference between the sum of digits at alternating places must be 0 or a multiple of 11.

Sum of odd-placed digits from the left = N + 1 + 2 = N + 3

Sum of even-placed digits from the left = 0 + M + 2 = M + 2

Difference = (M + 2) − (N + 3) = M − N − 1

Equating the difference to 0 for the lowest multiple of 11: M − N − 1 = 0 ⇒ M − N = 1

**∴ The correct answer is M − N = 1.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

A 6-digit number N01M22 is perfectly divisible by 11.

**Formula Used:**

A number is divisible by 11 if the difference between the sum of its digits at odd places and the sum of its digits at even places is either 0 or a multiple of 11.

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let us calculate the sum of the digits at odd positions (1st, 3rd, and 5th from the left).

⇒ Sₒdd = N + 1 + 2 = N + 3

⇒ Let us calculate the sum of the digits at even positions (2nd, 4th, and 6th from the left).

⇒ Sₑvₑₙ = 0 + M + 2 = M + 2

⇒ Now, find the difference between the even-placed sum and the odd-placed sum.

⇒ Difference = Sₑvₑₙ − Sₒdd = (M + 2) − (N + 3) = M − N − 1

⇒ For the number to be divisible by 11, this difference must be exactly 0, 11, or −11.

⇒ Case 1: M − N − 1 = 0 ⇒ M − N = 1 (This is a valid relation for single digits)

⇒ Case 2: M − N − 1 = 11 ⇒ M − N = 12 (Not possible since M and N are single digits and their maximum possible difference is 9)

⇒ Case 3: M − N − 1 = −11 ⇒ M − N = −10 (Not possible as the minimum difference can be −9)

⇒ Thus, the only feasible and correct relation is M − N = 1.

**∴ The correct answer is M − N = 1.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Divisibility Rule of 3 & 9

A number is divisible by 3 or 9 if the sum of all its digits is divisible by 3 or 9, respectively.

Divisibility Rule of 4 & 8

A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number that is divisible by 4. It is divisible by 8 if its last three digits are divisible by 8.

Combined Divisibility Rule of 7, 11, and 13

Group the digits in blocks of 3 starting from right to left. If the difference between the sums of the alternating blocks is exactly divisible by 7, 11, or 13, then the number is divisible by 7, 11, or 13 respectively.
